analysis.one_liner: Forces big election spenders to name their top funders within 24 hours and bars large federal contractors from campaign ads.
analysis.headline: The House passed the DISCLOSE Act 219-206 on June 24, 2010, but the Senate never took a final vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision opened the door for corporations and unions to spend on elections, this bill would have required any group spending more than $10,000 on campaign ads to report it within 24 hours and name its major funders. It would also have barred federal contractors with contracts of $10 million or more, bailout recipients, and companies negotiating offshore oil leases from electioneering, and extended the existing ban on foreign money to American subsidiaries controlled from abroad. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote, but the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never came to a final vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Anyone who sees a political ad on TV, radio, or the internet would have been able to look up within a day who paid for it, because spenders over $10,000 would have had to file a public report within 24 hours and ads would have to identify their top funders. It also would have curbed the most direct channels of influence-buying: companies with large federal contracts, firms that took bailout money, and companies negotiating offshore drilling leases would have been barred from election spending, and foreign-controlled domestic corporations would have been subject to the same ban on foreign political money as foreign companies.

how_it_helps.text: Any person or group making independent expenditures over $10,000 would have to file an electronic report within 24 hours, with the information posted publicly on the FEC website in a downloadable, searchable form, and file again after each additional $10,000 (or $1,000 within 20 days of an election).

Radio and TV electioneering ads would have to include statements identifying the groups paying for them and their significant funders, and covered organizations would have to report donors of $600 or more who gave for campaign purposes and post links to their FEC filings on their own websites.

Government contractors with contracts of $10 million or more, recipients of Troubled Asset Relief Program assistance, and companies negotiating for offshore oil and gas leases would have been prohibited from making independent expenditures, electioneering communications, or political contributions while those arrangements were in force.

The ban on foreign nationals' election spending would have been extended to domestic corporations controlled from abroad, with the CEO required to certify compliance to the FEC before any election spending.
Payments for campaign ads made in coordination with a candidate or party would have counted as contributions subject to limits, closing a route around contribution caps.
Registered lobbyists would have had to report their own independent expenditures and electioneering communications of $1,000 or more.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, trade associations, and tax-exempt groups that spend on elections would have borne new compliance and disclosure costs, and lost the ability to keep their funders hidden. Government contractors above $10 million, TARP recipients, and offshore lease negotiators would have lost the ability to spend on elections at all during those arrangements. Very large membership organizations, by contrast, were carved out of donor disclosure.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempted 501(c)(4) organizations with at least 500,000 dues-paying members in every state and no more than 15 percent corporate funding from the donor-disclosure rules, so the very largest membership organizations could keep their funders secret while smaller groups had to name theirs.

Rather than prohibiting corporate treasury spending on elections, the bill created optional 'Campaign-Related Activity Accounts' under which corporations and unions could keep electioneering from their general funds as long as they disclosed funders, which critics saw as legitimizing the post-Citizens United spending it was meant to answer.

The bill gave Members of Congress standing to sue over its constitutionality in a single court, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, a channel opponents targeted in a failed motion to recommit that won 208 votes, including 37 Democrats.
Disclosure rules would have applied to charities, unions, and trade associations alike, imposing compliance costs on smaller nonprofits even when their political spending was minor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: voters would have known who was paying for campaign ads within a day, instead of months or never. The design has genuine flaws, chiefly the carve-out that let the biggest membership organizations hide their funders while smaller groups had to disclose, and the choice to regulate corporate spending by disclosure rather than prohibition. Even with those compromises, the disclosure net it would have cast was far wider than anything in current law, so the benefit to voters outweighs the compliance costs, though the exemption blunted the bill's reach at exactly the point where hidden money is most concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House 219-206 on June 24, 2010, was read twice in the Senate and placed on the calendar, but after a July attempt to cut off debate fell one vote short of the 60 needed, no final vote was ever taken and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Administration Committee held hearings on May 6 and May 11, marked the bill up on May 20, and reported it amended on May 25; the Judiciary Committee was discharged the same day.
On June 24, 2010, a Republican motion to recommit with instructions to replace section 401 failed 208-217, with 37 Democrats and 171 Republicans voting for it.
The bill passed the House later that day 219-206, with 217 Democrats and 2 Republicans in favor and 170 Republicans and 36 Democrats opposed.

The Senate received the bill on June 28, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 448; no further action appears in the record before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, trade groups, and other big election spenders who can keep their funders undisclosed, and the incumbents of both parties who benefit from spending that voters cannot trace.

for.name: Rep. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the House as its lead sponsor.

for.name: House Committee on House Administration
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on May 6 and May 11, marked the bill up on May 20, and reported it amended on May 25, 2010.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the Senate floor in July 2010 and forced a vote to end debate, which fell short.

against.name: Rep. Daniel Lungren
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to strike section 401 (the judicial-review provision) and replace it; the motion failed 208-217.

against.name: 39 of 40 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted in July 2010 to block the bill from proceeding to a final vote, denying the 60 votes needed to end debate.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 217 of 255 voting Democrats backed passage while only 2 of 172 voting Republicans did, though 36 Democrats also voted no and 37 Democrats joined the Republican motion to recommit; the Senate fight split by party as well.

industries.note: The bill would have forced public, 24-hour disclosure of their election spending and major funders, but it also expressly preserved their right to electioneer from general treasury funds through disclosed accounts rather than banning it. Their interest in keeping funders hidden ran against voters' interest in knowing who pays for the ads they see.

industries.industry: Government contractors, TARP recipients, and offshore oil and gas leaseholders
industries.note: They would have been barred outright from campaign ads and contributions while their contracts, bailout assistance, or lease negotiations were active. The prohibition targeted the direct pipeline between federal dollars and political spending.

industries.industry: Trade associations and tax-exempt issue groups (501(c)(4), (5), (6) and 527 organizations)
industries.note: As covered organizations they would have had to name donors of $600 or more who gave for campaign purposes and disclose transfers to other groups for electioneering, ending the anonymity that makes 'dark money' ads possible.

Organizations with at least 500,000 dues-paying members in every state and little corporate funding were exempted from donor disclosure, so the largest and best-known groups could keep spending without naming funders while smaller groups had to comply.

Unions were covered organizations subject to the same funder-disclosure rules as corporations, and 36 House Democrats voted against the bill, though unions also faced the same post-Citizens United spending environment the bill was written for.

The existing ban on foreign political money would have applied to American subsidiaries controlled from abroad, with CEO certification to the FEC. Ordinary voters share the interest in keeping foreign governments and companies out of U.S. elections.
